sections.name: Cold open
lines: title
On the evening before the launch, a group of engineers in Utah tried to stop it.
meeting
They told NASA, on a conference call, that the space shuttle Challenger should not fly in the cold that was forecast for the next morning.
shuttle
By the next morning, their recommendation had been reversed. Challenger launched at eleven thirty-eight a.m. on the twenty-eighth of January, 1986.
shuttle
Seventy-three seconds later, millions of people watched it break apart in the sky.
lesson

lines.text: The warning was given. It was not heard.

lines: This is not a story about a failure nobody saw coming. It is a story about a warning that was given, clearly, the night before, and about how it was talked away.

sections.name: The mission
lines: date
The mission was called S T S fifty-one L. It was the twenty-fifth flight of the space shuttle programme, and Challenger's tenth.
people

There were seven people aboard. Commander Dick Scobee. Pilot Michael Smith. Mission specialists Ellison Onizuka, Judith Resnik and Ronald McNair. Payload specialist Gregory Jarvis. And Christa McAuliffe.
portrait

lines.name: Christa McAuliffe
lines.role: Teacher in Space · Concord, New Hampshire

lines: McAuliffe was a high school social studies teacher from New Hampshire, chosen from more than eleven thousand applicants to be the first teacher in space. Schoolchildren across America would be watching the launch live in their classrooms.
lesson

lines.text: NASA had promised a launch almost every two weeks.

lines: NASA was under pressure. It had promised Congress that the shuttle would fly often and cheaply, almost like an airline. In 1986 it planned a record fifteen flights. Challenger's launch had already been delayed several times.
date

On the twenty-seventh, the crew had already been strapped in. Then the countdown was stopped, first by a stuck bolt on the hatch handle, and then by strong crosswinds. The launch was moved to the next morning.

sections.name: The joint
lines: shuttle
The shuttle was launched by two solid rocket boosters, strapped to the sides of a huge external fuel tank. Each booster was built in sections, stacked on top of each other and joined together.
oring
Each joint was sealed by two rubber rings, called O-rings, that were supposed to stop burning gas at thousands of degrees from escaping through the gap.
oring

On earlier flights, engineers had found that hot gas had sometimes got past the first ring and scorched it. The worst damage had come on a flight launched in January 1985, in the coldest weather the shuttle had flown in. The temperature at launch was fifty-three degrees Fahrenheit.
shuttle

The boosters were recovered from the ocean after every flight and taken apart, so engineers could see exactly what had happened inside each joint. They kept finding soot and burned rubber where none should have been.
portrait

Roger Boisjoly was an engineer at Morton Thiokol, the company in Utah that built the boosters. In July 1985, he wrote a memo warning that if the problem was not fixed, the result could be a catastrophe of the highest order, loss of human life.
oring

The physics was simple. Rubber gets stiff when it is cold. A stiff O-ring takes longer to spring into the gap and seal it, and in a rocket booster, a fraction of a second is enough for hot gas to get past.
lesson

But every time a shuttle came back safely, the damage was treated less as a warning, and more as an accepted risk. A sociologist who later studied the disaster gave this a name: the normalisation of deviance.

sections.name: The night before
lines: shuttle
On the twenty-seventh of January, an unusual cold front swept across Florida. Overnight temperatures were forecast to drop well below freezing.
meeting

lines.text: We have never flown this cold.

lines: That evening, engineers at Thiokol asked for a teleconference with NASA managers in Florida and Alabama. They faxed over their charts.
meeting
Their recommendation was not to launch if the temperature was below fifty-three degrees, the coldest launch they had any experience of.
meeting

lines.text: When do you want me to launch, next April?

lines: NASA's managers pushed back hard. The data, they said, did not prove that cold caused the damage. One of them asked, in frustration, when Thiokol wanted him to launch. Next April?
meeting

lines.text: Take off your engineering hat and put on your management hat.

lines: Thiokol asked for a few minutes off the line. In that private meeting, a senior manager told the head of engineering to take off his engineering hat, and put on his management hat.
meeting

When the call resumed, Thiokol's managers reversed the recommendation. The engineers were not asked to vote. NASA accepted the new advice, and the people above them were never told how fierce the argument had been.
portrait

lines.name: Allan McDonald
lines.role: Thiokol's senior representative at Kennedy Space Center

lines: In Florida, Thiokol's senior man at the Cape, Allan McDonald, refused to sign the written recommendation to launch. His boss in Utah signed it instead.
portrait

lines.name: Roger Boisjoly
lines.role: “I fought like hell to stop that launch.”

lines: Boisjoly later said he went home that night convinced the shuttle would explode on the pad.

sections.name: Launch morning
lines: shuttle

On the morning of the twenty-eighth, there was ice on the launch tower. Long icicles hung from the gantry. At liftoff, the air temperature was thirty-six degrees Fahrenheit, seventeen degrees colder than any previous launch.
people

lines.label: the ice team on the pad

lines: An ice inspection team walked the pad before dawn. Engineers from Rockwell, the company that built the orbiter, said they could not be sure falling ice would not damage the shuttle at launch. But they did not formally ask for a stop. Nobody discussed the boosters' O-rings.
clock
At eleven thirty-eight, Challenger left the pad.
shuttle
In the first second after ignition, cameras recorded puffs of dark grey smoke from the aft joint of the right booster. The cold O-rings had not sealed. Burning gas was escaping.
oring
For a while, by luck, the hole was plugged by melted residue from the burning fuel itself. The shuttle climbed normally.
shuttle

About a minute after launch, the shuttle flew through strong wind shear. The seal broke open again. A flame appeared at the joint, and played across the strut holding the booster to the external tank.
clock
Seventy-three seconds after liftoff, the tank failed. The booster swung loose, and the shuttle was torn apart by aerodynamic forces.
shuttle
On television, a cloud spread across the sky, with the two boosters flying off on their own. For a long moment, the commentator said nothing.
lesson

lines.text: The crew cabin fell for nearly three minutes.

lines: The crew cabin broke away largely intact and fell to the ocean. Evidence recovered later suggested that some of the crew were alive and conscious for at least part of the fall. None could have survived the impact.

sections.name: The commission
lines: inquiry

lines.label: Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident · 1986

lines: President Reagan appointed a commission, led by former Secretary of State William Rogers, to find out what had happened.
portrait

lines.name: Richard Feynman
lines.role: Physicist · member of the Rogers Commission

lines: One of its members was the physicist Richard Feynman. At a televised hearing, he took a piece of O-ring rubber, squeezed it in a clamp, and dropped it into a glass of ice water.
oring
When he took it out, it stayed squeezed. It did not spring back. In a few seconds, he had shown what the engineers had tried to explain the night before.
lesson
In his own appendix to the report, Feynman wrote that for a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.
timeline

The commission found a flawed joint design, known for years. Damage that had been accepted as normal. Pressure to keep to the schedule. And a decision-making process in which serious warnings never reached the people at the top.

sections.name: After
lines: stat
The shuttle fleet was grounded for thirty-two months. The boosters were redesigned, with a third O-ring and heaters at the joints. NASA created a new office of safety.
portrait

Roger Boisjoly and Allan McDonald told the commission what had happened on the call. Afterwards, both were moved away from the work they knew best. Boisjoly left the company, and spent years speaking to engineering students about ethics and the duty to speak up.
lesson

But the deeper problem proved harder to fix. In 2003, the shuttle Columbia broke up on its way home, after foam struck its wing during launch. Foam strikes had happened before. They had come to be seen as normal. The investigators said the lessons of Challenger had not been learned.
people
Seven people died on Challenger. The engineers who had tried to stop the launch spent the rest of their lives asking whether they could have done more.
lesson

The warning had been right. It had been made clearly, by the people who knew the most. It lost, because it could not prove, with certainty, that disaster would come. It only showed that nobody knew it would not.
memorial
When an organisation demands proof that something is dangerous, rather than proof that it is safe, it has already made its decision.
